sections.heading: Frame definitions and units
sections.body: A pinhole camera is attached to a square rover plate. For this sheet the base frame B has x forward, y left and z upward. Define a camera carrier C, with its x axis pointing left in B and its y axis pointing backward. Its z axis points upward. The origin of C in B coordinates is (0.24, -0.08, 0.36) metres. An observed marker A has coordinates (0.10, 0.04, -0.12) metres in C.

sections.heading: 1. Draw the physical frames
sections.body: Draw a plan view of B and C and mark their origins. On a second sketch, show the two z axes and the signed height of A above the base. Give the coordinates of C’s three unit directions in B and state whether the directions form a right-handed basis.

sections.heading: 2. Compose the rigid change of coordinates
sections.body: Use the directions as the columns of a matrix mapping C coordinates into B. Write out the homogeneous transform and apply it to marker A. Test the transform with the origin of C and with a second point one metre along its x axis. Turn in the matrix, the two tests, and the marker coordinates with units.

sections.heading: 3. Trace a bad calibration
sections.body: Another student has put -0.08 in the first translation slot and 0.24 in the second. Pick a point that exposes this error without changing the rotation, then explain why testing only a vector with homogeneous w = 0 would miss it. Present one numerical counterexample and a two-sentence diagnosis.

sections.heading: Comparison with the physical mount
sections.body: Set a ruler along the camera carrier x axis and imagine moving the observed marker 0.05 m along that ruler. Give the change in the base coordinates without recalculating the entire transform. As a hand check, your answer should be a direction vector with length 0.05 m. On your drawing distinguish motion of the observed marker from motion of the camera mount; the two cases change different terms in the transformation.

prediction.explanation: Two physical runs plus exporting bumper edges.

pdf.title: Dock approach and bumper taps on cart C

sections.heading: Capture the two traversals
sections.body: Place the foam dock at the tape line. Record the bumper switch, both wheel tick streams, and the odometry topic before the robot moves. Run the forward approach until the tape marker meets the dock edge. Mark that approximate meeting time in the operator note. Reverse until the two switches clear and keep the recorder going through the short stationary tail.

sections.heading: Required outputs
sections.body: Keep separate bag names for each traversal. Export a graph with time since first tick on the horizontal axis and label the first bumper closure and last opening. Repeat the test when any required stream never publishes. Include a small table of consecutive edge timestamps so the reader can tell switch bounce from the genuine release.

rows: false to true near foam dock

sections.heading: Sign the log
sections.body: Record whether the foam dock moved and which approach bag was used for the final plot. If the control laptop changes during the run, record the device name and bag start as captured on that laptop. Keep incomplete bags with an INCOMPLETE suffix.

sections.heading: A bounce that looks like a second approach
sections.body: A left-switch trace may contain 0, 1, 0, 1 in four adjacent rows while the right switch stays at 1 and the wheel counts show no reversal. Present that window as supporting data and indicate how you decided whether the final opening was genuine. Do not remove the raw edges from the exported trace; annotate your decision in a separate column.

holdouts.title: Record the cable-cover crossing on rover C
holdouts.description: Collect two real crossings of the rubber cable cover, compare IMU spikes and wheel speeds, and deliver the annotated plots.
holdouts.details: Use club rover C with its original USB bridge. The mat and laptop are already set up.
holdouts.check: The three physical rover-C sessions with the old USB bridge took 63/40, 77/50 and 70/45. This physical trace session took 71/45. Offline bag replay has no reconnection or rerun burden.

evaluation.rationale: The three physical rover-C sessions with the old USB bridge took 63/40, 77/50 and 70/45. This physical trace session took 71/45. Offline bag replay has no reconnection or rerun burden.

expected_caution.rationale: Warn that the original USB bridge disconnected on earlier live captures; leave time to reconnect and repeat the affected run.

sections.heading: Question and physical layout
sections.body: Does the wheel-speed estimate change at the same instant as the inertial peak when the front casters reach a rubber cable cover? Work on the marked straight course. Place the 16 mm cover at the central tape line and leave the landing strip clear. Use the same driven wheel pair, tire pressure and laptop for both trials. Do not swap left and right sensor names between runs.

sections.heading: Two comparable observations
sections.body: With the rover stationary, start the recorder before the approach. Perform two passes in the same direction at the club’s marked crawl setting. End each bag after the rear wheel clears the cover. Count a pass as complete only when wheel and inertial data span the approach, crossing, and landing. Write down any manual steering correction; that is a limitation of the trial.

sections.heading: Channels and time bases
sections.body: Wheel counters and IMU samples carry sensor timestamps; bag arrival time may lag. Use the stamp inside the message when the field exists. Retain the raw value and its units in your exported table.

sections.heading: Pull the crossing from the trace
sections.body: Start with the manual crossing mark, find the vertical acceleration peak in a small neighborhood, and compare it with the change in wheel speed. Keep the two original time series and the aligned copy. In the example below the wheel samples are less frequent than inertial samples. The nearest arrival record is not necessarily the nearest sensor-time record.
sections.code:
stream        sensor stamp (s)    sample
left wheel        12.360           1,392 ticks
imu.z             12.371          11.8 m/s^2
imu.z             12.381          15.1 m/s^2
left wheel        12.400           1,400 ticks

sections.heading: Plot and recovery checks
sections.body: Overlay both wheel speeds above the inertial trace, with separate panels for passes A and B. Label the same event in each panel. If a topic disappears halfway through, keep the partial bag under a new name and repeat the affected pass. A partial run must never silently become a zero-speed segment in the final graph.

sections.heading: Hand-in to the club notebook
sections.body: Include raw bag identifiers, a small CSV excerpt containing the crossing, two annotated plots and a paragraph on the lag between peaks. Note sensor-frame orientation and whether correcting the baseline changed the selected peak. Leave the mat and course tape as found.

sections.heading: Compare across passes
sections.body: Compute the signed difference between wheel-speed change and acceleration peak for each pass. Write the sign convention in the column header. If one pass reverses the order of events, inspect raw message sequence numbers and overlapping sample intervals before calling it a physical lead or lag. Report when the sampling interval is larger than the claimed difference.

holdouts.title: Plot the ramp trial from yesterday’s recording
holdouts.description: Replay the ramp bag on the laptop, mark the two wheel-slip events and export the overlays.
holdouts.details: The archive is saved locally. This is offline analysis only; no rover or bridge is required.
holdouts.check: Two earlier archived-bag tasks finished near their guesses (42/45 and 36/35). The laptop-only ramp analysis took 38/40. A warning to reconnect the live robot would be out of scope.

evaluation.rationale: Two earlier archived-bag tasks finished near their guesses (42/45 and 36/35). The laptop-only ramp analysis took 38/40. A warning to reconnect the live robot would be out of scope.

sections.heading: Archive contents
sections.body: The completed run is in ramp_B_12. The bag includes two wheel counters, motor current and the operator marks at the entry/exit tape. All three series are timestamped by the logger on the cart. The setup photo and a separate timing note are in the same local folder. No acquisition or new run is part of this analysis.

sections.heading: Inspect before plotting
sections.body: The wheel channel wraps at 65536. Construct differences between consecutive samples before smoothing and handle a negative wrap when the next value is near zero. Mark a candidate slip only inside the interval from entering to leaving the ramp. Compare the raw count differences to the current peak to rule out a split record.

sections.heading: Deliver the overlays
sections.body: Show an unfiltered trace and a clearly labeled smoothed trace on common axes. Number the two slip events in capture order. Write which sample adjacent to each peak you used and why; a reviewer should be able to recover both markers from the archived bag.

sections.heading: Diagnostic ambiguity
sections.body: A learner treated the span between counts 65530 and 3 as a large negative speed. Derive the forward difference for that span, state the wrap assumption explicitly, and place that result beside the uncorrected speed on the diagnostic plot. A second pass near a direction change may violate the forward-motion assumption; explain how you would decide using the sign of the other wheel and the operator mark.
